text: Homes can have all kinds of insurance. There's flood insurance, to cover flood damages, there's homeowners insurance to cover the property and the valuables inside the home. If you wanted to, you could live without insurance - it's not like auto insurance where you're required to have it if you're driving on the road. Of course, if something happens to your house, you're screwed. Also, if you don't have a million dollars or so of cash burning a hole in your pocket, a bank will have to issue you a loan to cover the cost of the house. The bank will force you to have insurance as some of the terms for a loan. If you live in a condo, the condo association will probably also require you to have insurance in case there's a fire in your condo or something and it damages someone else's condo in the building. Basically - you need insurance. Once Iniki hit, the insurance companies had to pay out a ton of money for all of the claims that were filed. That's literally the purpose of insurance. So let's say you had a $500k home that's now a total loss. They'd have to give you the $500k to rebuild it. Insurance companies don't like losing money. (From a cynic's view, insurance companies are like "the house" in a casino. They'll lose money here and there, but overall they're charging their customers more than they're paying out. A bankrupt insurance company can't pay claims after all) So after they paid out, they all pulled out of Hawaii. You couldn't find an insurance company to issue you a policy on your home. So banks couldn't issue mortgages, and homeowners (and potential homeowners) were stuck. So the state came in, seeded their own insurance company with state money, and began issuing policies and charging folks a normal rate. In a few years, the insurance companies came back, and folks didn't have to use the hurricane relief fund any more. So the money that was there sat idly. (On a side note, you had people asking for that money back. That's like asking your insurance company for your premiums back.) Hopefully that was clear

text: Lahaina is a National Historic District. While we are all dealing with a complex set of emotions processing what happened to Lahaina and what may yet come with the rebuild, I'd like to offer a bit of good news for those worried that a rebuilt Lahaina will lose all of it's character. Thankfully it's a National Historic District and [has been since 1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahaina_Historic_District). That's what has helped it maintain is character and charm all these decades. What does that mean for the rebuild? A lot of that will be determined by local ordinances already in place and ongoing community engagement. But the historic district designation will absolutely make sure that a lot of attention is placed on the history and architectural character of the rebuild. You can't truly replace a lot of what was lost, but I'm hopeful a lot of what comes next won't be unrecognizable to what was there before. Historic preservation as a science and an industry is pretty mature. There are plenty of examples of historic buildings being lost to fire and rebuilt, but an entire district being lost is another matter. A lot of federal support is needed. If you feel like making your voice heard on the matter you should contact the [senate](https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/subcommittees/interior-environment-and-related-agencies) and [house](https://appropriations.house.gov/subcommittees/interior-environment-and-related-agencies-118th-congress) committees governing the Dept. of Interior and National Park Service. That being said, this is of secondary concern to all those who lost loved ones and the now unhoused people who need care and support. Rebuilding the workforce housing will be an even bigger lift. But we can do all of it because it is all worth doing

text: I’m sure there will be a full investigative report, but from what I’ve read: It was the middle of the night, so people in town were asleep. The high winds meant that the firefighters couldn’t send a helicopter up to monitor the blaze, and the ones on the ground were struggling to keep up with it (because the single road around west Maui had fallen trees and debris impeding them). The winds carried embers a far distance and lit up west Maui far more quickly and intensely than anyone expected, and by the time they realized the town was in danger it was too late to respond. Cell towers were already down by that point too, there was no 911. Firefighters were overwhelmed by trying to clear the road to clear the path out for evacuees and to get themselves closer to the town. A call was made for the coast guard and anyone else with boats to try to rescue people in Lahaina. The reports coming out from survivors make it sound like the fire arrived extremely quickly and that they barely made it out in time

If the wind was blowing in a specific way certain buildings behind them could have been protected. Another area that didn't burn is a brand new development called Kohoma Village. Pure conjecture but could have had fire resistant materials used. If their shingles didn't burn that could have protected all the homes. Certain plants are fire resistant, some trees survive because they don't burn as easily as others do. So could theorize that a home surrounded by the right plants through sheer luck blocked sparks from hitting their home and had a domino effect
